title: Sibylla
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Aeneas passes the walls of Parthenope, comes ashore at Cumae and begs the Sibyl for a way down to his father; the god enters her, she promises him the underworld and shows him the golden bough. He obeys, sees the wealth of Orcus, his own forebears and the shade of Anchises, learns what dangers the wars ahead hold, and on the climb back offers her temples and incense. She refuses them, and tells him why: she is no goddess but a woman who asked Phoebus for as many birthdays as there were grains in a heap of dust, forgot to ask that they be young ones, and refused the price he set on youth — seven ages are behind her, three hundred harvests are still ahead, and at the end of them she will have shrunk past seeing, known by her voice alone.

sentences.t:
Has ubi praeteriit et Parthenopeia dextra
moenia deseruit, laeva de parte canori
Aeolidae tumulum et, loca feta palustribus undis,
litora Cumarum vivacisque antra Sibyllae
intrat, et ut manes veniat per Averna paternos,
orat.
sentences.l: When he had passed these by and left behind the Parthenopean walls on his right hand, on the left side he enters the tomb of the tuneful son of Aeolus and — places teeming with marshy waters — the shores of Cumae and the caves of the long-lived Sibyl, and he begs that he may come through the Avernan country to his father's shade.
sentences.i: When he had passed these and left the walls of Parthenope behind on his right, he came in on the left to the tomb of the tuneful son of Aeolus and to the shore of Cumae, a country teeming with marsh water, and to the cave of the Sibyl whose life goes on and on — and there he begged to go down through Avernus to his father's shade.
sentences.n: Has is an accusative plural with no noun in these lines: it points back to whatever the poem was listing before this part opens, and the reader arriving here is meant to be already moving. dextra is best taken as an ablative, “on the right hand”, balancing laeva de parte in the next line; it could formally be a neuter plural agreeing with moenia, “the right-hand walls”, but the answering phrase makes the ablative the natural reading. Parthenopeia moenia are the walls of Parthenope, the town later called Naples. canori Aeolidae is a genitive split across the line-end — canori closes 102, Aeolidae opens 103 — and it names nobody: “the tuneful son of Aeolus” is the trumpeter Misenus by the ordinary identification, and canorus, “tuneful”, is the epithet that gives him away. One verb, intrat, serves three accusatives — tumulum, litora, antra — and English feels the strain of “entering” a tomb and a shoreline: the verb is chosen for the cave at the end of the list. loca feta palustribus undis is dropped in as an apposition to litora, marked off by Magnus's commas; Magnus prints undis, “waters”, and some editions print ulvis, “sedge”, which makes the ground rank with marsh grass instead of standing water. vivacis, “long-lived”, is doing more than decoration — it is the whole of what she is about to tell. In 105 manes ... paternos is an accusative of the goal reached with no preposition, which verse allows; some editions read adeat for veniat, and adire takes that accusative as a matter of course.

sentences.t:
At illa diu vultum tellure moratum
erexit tandemque deo furibunda recepto
“magna petis” dixit, “vir factis maxime, cuius
dextera per ferrum est, pietas spectata per ignes.
sentences.l: But she raised her face, that had lingered long on the earth, and at last, with the god taken into her, raving, 'Great things you ask,' she said, 'man greatest in your deeds, whose right hand has been proved by the sword, whose devotion by fire.
sentences.i: But she lifted her face, which had stayed a long while turned to the ground, and at last, once the god was in her and the frenzy on her, 'It is a great thing you ask,' she said, 'greatest of men in what you have done, whose right hand has stood the test of the sword, and whose devotion the test of fire.
sentences.n: moratum is the perfect participle of the deponent moror, passive in form and active in meaning, “having lingered”, and it agrees with vultum: it is the face that lingers, not the woman, which is the Latin way of saying that she kept her eyes down. tellure is a bare ablative of place. deo ... recepto is an ablative absolute, “with the god taken in”, and the possession is described from the outside; furibunda, “raving”, is nominative and belongs to her. factis is an ablative of respect with maxime: greatest in the department of deeds. The last line shares its parts crosswise: cuius dextera per ferrum est borrows the participle spectata from the second limb, and pietas spectata per ignes borrows est from the first, so each half is complete only by the other. Magnus prints that est; some editions leave it out, and then neither limb has a finite verb of its own.

sentences.t: Pone tamen, Troiane, metum:
sentences.l: Yet lay aside your fear, Trojan:
sentences.i: Still, Trojan, put your fear away:
sentences.n: pone is the imperative of pono, which with metum has the settled sense “lay aside” rather than “put down”. tamen concedes what she has just said: the request is a great one, and she will grant it anyway. Troiane is a vocative, and she does not use his name at any point in her first speech — he is addressed by his deeds in 108 and by his people here. The colon is Magnus's, and it points forward: what follows is the reassurance itself.

sentences.t:
potiere petitis
Elysiasque domos et regna novissima mundi
me duce cognosces simulacraque cara parentis.
sentences.l: you will get possession of the things you asked for, and with me as leader you will come to know the Elysian houses and the world's last kingdoms and the dear likeness of your father.
sentences.i: you will have what you asked for; with me to lead you, you will come to know the houses of Elysium, the furthest kingdoms of the world, and the beloved shade of your father.
sentences.n: potiere is potieris, the alternative second-person ending: a future of the deponent potior, active in meaning, governing the ablative petitis. petitis is the perfect participle of peto used as a noun, “the things asked for”, and it picks up petis two lines earlier. me duce is an ablative absolute of the barest kind — two nouns and no participle, because Latin has no present participle of “to be” — so “with me as leader”. novissima is the superlative of novus in its other sense, “last, furthest”, not “newest”. simulacrum is an appearance without a body, and the plural here is the poetic plural for one father.

sentences.t: Invia virtuti nulla est via!”
sentences.l: No road is impassable to valour!'
sentences.i: There is no road valour cannot travel!'
sentences.n: The line is built on a jingle that English cannot quite keep: invia is in- plus via, so the Latin says “no way is un-way to valour”, with invia standing first in its clause and via last in it — Dixit et auro follows in the same verse — and the negative nulla and the verb shut between them. virtuti is a dative of the person or quality for whom a thing is or is not possible. virtus is not “virtue” in the modern moral sense but the quality of a vir: nerve, prowess, the willingness to go. The exclamation mark is Magnus's and closes her speech.

sentences.t:
Dixit et auro
fulgentem ramum silva Iunonis Avernae
monstravit iussitque suo divellere trunco.
sentences.l: She spoke, and showed the bough gleaming with gold in the wood of Avernal Juno, and ordered him to tear it from its own trunk.
sentences.i: So she spoke, and showed him the bough shining with gold in the grove of the Juno of Avernus, and told him to wrench it away from the trunk that bore it.
sentences.n: Iuno Averna, “Juno of Avernus”, is the queen of the underworld named by her office rather than her name. silva is a bare ablative of place, which verse allows without in, and auro fulgentem is an ablative of means, gleaming by reason of gold. divello is “tear apart, wrench away”, and suo ... trunco is an ablative of separation with the possessive carrying the point: the bough is being pulled off the trunk that owns it. iussit takes the infinitive with the person ordered left unexpressed, which English has to supply. These lines do not say what the golden bough is for or who requires it.

sentences.l: Aeneas obeyed, and saw the riches of dreadful Orcus and his own forefathers and the aged shade of great-souled Anchises;
sentences.i: Aeneas obeyed, and he saw the wealth of dreadful Orcus, and his own ancestors, and the shade of great-hearted Anchises in its old age;
sentences.n: Two verbs carry this whole unit, paruit and vidit, and vidit has three objects: opes, atavos, umbram. formidabilis Orci fills the end of 116 and the noun it depends on, opes, arrives in 117 only after the verb. Orcus is the underworld and its god at once; opes is “resources, wealth”, so the dead are counted as the holdings of a rich house. atavus is strictly a great-great-great-grandfather and is used loosely for the line of forebears. senilem is transferred: it is the shade that is called aged, and the point is that the dead keep the age they died at. magnanimus is a heroic epithet, “great-souled”. Anchises is a Greek name taken into the Latin first declension: the nominative keeps its Greek -es, but the genitive Anchisae is the ordinary Latin first-declension ending and not a Greek form. The semicolon is Magnus's, and it separates what Aeneas saw from what he learned.

sentences.t:
didicit quoque iura locorum,
quaeque novis essent adeunda pericula bellis.
sentences.l: he learned too the laws of those places, and what dangers were to be faced in new wars.
sentences.i: and he learned as well the rules that hold down there, and what dangers he would have to meet in the wars still to come.
sentences.n: quoque is the adverb “also”, not quo with -que. iura locorum is “the law of the places”, what holds good there. The -que on quaeque joins a second object to iura, and quae ... pericula opens an indirect question, which is why essent is subjunctive. essent adeunda is the passive periphrastic, gerundive plus esse: what has to be gone through. adire is “go to, face”. novis and bellis are pulled apart, novis standing second in the line and bellis held back to its last word, with essent adeunda pericula shut between them; the phrase can be read two ways: as a dative of agent with the gerundive, which oddly makes the wars the agent, or, more easily, as an ablative of the circumstances, “in new wars”. The Latin does not decide.

sentences.t:
Inde ferens lassos adverso tramite passus
cum duce Cumaea mollit sermone laborem.
sentences.l: From there, carrying weary steps up the path that faced him, with his Cumaean guide he softens the toil with talk.
sentences.i: From there, dragging tired feet up the climb, he eased the labour with talk as he went beside his Cumaean guide.
sentences.n: ferens ... passus is the Latin idiom of “bearing one's steps” for walking, and lassos, “weary”, is fastened to the steps rather than to the man. adverso tramite is an ablative of the road taken; adversus is “facing, coming against”, so the track is the one that meets him — the climb back. Magnus prints adverso; some editions print averso, “by a path turned away”, which sends him back by some other road rather than up the same one. mollit is a present standing among the perfects around it (paruit, vidit, didicit): Latin narrative slips into the present to bring an action close, and these lines do it again at carpit in 122 and respicit in 129. She is called dux Cumaea here and virgo Cumaea at 135 — named by her town both times.

sentences.t:
Dumque iter horrendum per opaca crepuscula carpit,
“seu dea tu praesens, seu dis gratissima” dixit,
“numinis instar eris semper mihi meque fatebor
muneris esse tui, quae me loca mortis adire,
quae loca me visae voluisti evadere mortis.
sentences.l: And while he plucks his way along the dreadful road through the dim twilight, 'Whether you are a goddess present in person, or one most pleasing to the gods,' he said, 'you will always be to me the equal of a divine power, and I shall confess that I am a thing of your gift — you who willed me to go to the places of death, who willed me to escape the places of the death I had seen.
sentences.i: And as he made his way along that horrible road through the dark half-light, 'Whether you are a goddess here in your own person,' he said, 'or a woman dearest of all to the gods, you will always stand to me for a god, and I shall own that I owe what I am to your gift — you who willed that I should go into the country of death, and willed that I should come out of the country of death, once I had seen it.
sentences.n: carpere iter is the standing idiom, “to pluck one's way”, for travelling, and carpit is another present in a past narrative. seu ... seu puts two possibilities and settles neither: praesens of a god means present and at work, not merely nearby, so the first limb makes her a goddess on the spot and the second demotes her to a mortal favourite. instar is an indeclinable neuter noun taking a genitive, “the equal of”, used here as a predicate. fatebor governs an accusative and infinitive, me ... esse, with muneris ... tui a predicate genitive: literally “that I am of your gift”, the genitive of the thing one belongs to. quae, twice over, picks up tu, and both clauses lean on the one verb voluisti in 126, which English has to state twice — the first of them has no finite verb of its own. That last line is interlocked as far as Latin will go: loca and mortis are separated by four words, and visae, agreeing with mortis, stands between me and voluisti.

sentences.t:
Pro quibus aerias meritis evectus ad auras
templa tibi statuam, tribuam tibi turis honores.”
sentences.l: In return for which services, once I have been carried up to the airy breezes, I shall set up temples to you, I shall grant you the honours of incense.'
sentences.i: And for these kindnesses, when I have been carried back up into the open air, I will raise you temples and give you the honour of incense.'
sentences.n: pro quibus ... meritis is a connecting relative: Latin opens a new sentence with a relative where English wants “and for these”, and the idiomatic layer here does exactly that while the literal keeps the Latin shape. evectus is the perfect participle of eveho and is passive: one does not climb out of the underworld, one is carried up out of it. aerias ... ad auras alliterates, and the adjective is cut off from its noun by meritis and evectus. The two futures statuam and tribuam stand side by side with no conjunction, and tibi is repeated in both halves: the promise is made twice in one breath. turis honores is a genitive of what the honour consists of — burnt incense — and it is precisely what she refuses in the next unit.

sentences.l: The prophetess looks back at him and, with sighs drawn up, 'I am not a goddess,' she said, 'nor hold a human head worthy of the honour of holy incense;
sentences.i: The prophetess turned and looked at him and, drawing her sighs up from the bottom of her, 'I am no goddess,' she said, 'and do not count a mortal head worth the honour of holy incense;
sentences.n: vates is the word for a prophet who speaks in verse, seer and poet at once, and it is the first time these lines call her that: she has been Sibylla at 104 and dux Cumaea at 121. suspiratibus haustis is an ablative absolute; haurio is “draw up, drain”, used of drawing water, so the sighs are pulled up from the bottom of her. dignare is the imperative of the deponent dignor, passive in form and active in meaning, “hold worthy”; it takes the accusative humanum ... caput and the ablative honore. nec with an imperative is a negative command in the older, higher style, where prose would use noli. caput, “head”, stands for the whole person, and humanum sets it against the dea she has just refused to be.

sentences.t:
neu nescius erres,
lux aeterna mihi carituraque fine dabatur,
si mea virginitas Phoebo patuisset amanti.
sentences.l: and so that you may not go astray in ignorance: everlasting light, and light that would lack an end, was being given to me, if my maidenhood had lain open to Phoebus, who was in love with me.
sentences.i: and so you are not left mistaken: everlasting light, light that would never come to an end, was being held out to me — if I had opened my virginity to Phoebus, who was in love with me.
sentences.n: neu, which is neve, introduces a negative purpose clause after the imperative, with erres in the subjunctive; nescius, “not knowing”, is nominative and agrees with the subject of erres, so the ignorance is his. lux aeterna is everlasting light, that is, life without end, and the -que adds a second description of the same thing: caritura is the future participle of careo, which governs the ablative fine, “about to lack an end”. dabatur is imperfect indicative and not subjunctive, and the choice matters: the offer was really on the table and being made, and only the condition attached to it went unfulfilled, which is why si ... patuisset is pluperfect subjunctive. pateo is “stand open”, and the phrase is the euphemism the Latin itself uses; it is kept here rather than sharpened or softened. amanti is the present participle of amo agreeing with Phoebo.

sentences.t:
Dum tamen hanc sperat dum praecorrumpere donis
me cupit, “elige” ait, “virgo Cumaea, quid optes:
sentences.l: Yet while he hopes for this, while he wants to buy me in advance with gifts, 'Choose,' he says, 'maiden of Cumae, what you would wish for:
sentences.i: But while he was still hoping for it, while he was set on buying me first with presents, 'Choose,' he says, 'girl of Cumae, whatever you want:
sentences.n: hanc has no noun with it and reaches back to virginitas in the line before: “this” is what he is still hoping for. The two dum clauses stand side by side with nothing joining them and Magnus prints no comma between them, so the repeated dum does the joining on its own. praecorrumpere is corrumpo with prae-, “bribe in advance” — the gift is meant to buy the thing before it is asked for. ait is a defective verb surviving in a handful of forms and is the ordinary way of quoting speech. elige is the imperative of eligo, “pick out”, and quid optes is an indirect question depending on it, hence the subjunctive. She names herself as the god named her, virgo Cumaea, by her town, as she was dux Cumaea at 121. Magnus marks the god's words with the same double quotation marks as her own speech, which is still open from 130, so the quotation inside the quotation is not typographically distinguished.

sentences.t: optatis potiere tuis.”
sentences.l: you shall have possession of your wishes.'
sentences.i: what you choose, you shall have.'
sentences.n: potiere is potieris again, the same future of the deponent potior with the same alternative ending, governing the ablative optatis tuis, the perfect participle of opto used as a noun: “the things wished for”. The god's guarantee is the same verb she herself used to Aeneas at 110, potiere petitis — the formula that was a comfort there is the trap here, and she is quoting it back into her own story.

sentences.t:
Ego pulveris hausti
ostendi cumulum:
sentences.l: I showed a heap of dust that had been scooped up:
sentences.i: I held up a heap of dust I had scooped:
sentences.n: Ego is written out and stands first: Latin does not need the pronoun, so it is emphatic — the choosing was hers. pulveris hausti is a genitive depending on cumulum, and hausti is the perfect passive participle of haurio, the same participle that was used of her sighs at 129, there in the ablative plural, here in its plain sense of scooping something up. Magnus prints the finite ostendi, “I showed”; some editions print the participle ostendens, “showing”, which leaves the whole sentence hanging on rogavi in 138. The colon is Magnus's and makes what follows the content of the wish.

sentences.t:
quot haberet corpora pulvis,
tot mihi natales contingere vana rogavi;
sentences.l: as many bodies as the dust held, so many birthdays to fall to me — empty-headed, I asked;
sentences.i: I asked that as many birthdays should fall to me as there were grains in the dust — and I was a fool;
sentences.n: quot ... tot is the ordinary correlative pair, “as many ... so many”. haberet is subjunctive because the clause stands inside what she asked for; English has no way of marking that, and the literal renders it plainly. corpora is literally “bodies”, used of the smallest particles of matter, so “grains”. contingere is the infinitive of an accusative and infinitive after rogavi, and contingo with a dative is “fall to someone's lot”, generally of good fortune, which is where the irony sits. natales are birthdays, years counted by their returns rather than by their length. vana is most naturally a nominative feminine agreeing with the speaker, thrown in beside the verb: “empty-headed, I asked” — vanus is both silly and futile and both senses are live. It could instead be a neuter plural object of rogavi, “I asked for empty things”; the accusative and infinitive already supplies an object, which is why the nominative reading is preferred here.

sentences.t: excidit, ut peterem iuvenes quoque protinus annos.
sentences.l: It slipped out of my mind, that I should ask also for years that stayed young without a break.
sentences.i: What escaped me was to ask, as well, for years that would go on being young.
sentences.n: excido is “fall out”, used absolutely of a thing that drops out of the mind; the ut clause that follows is what fell out, so it works as the subject of the verb. peterem is imperfect subjunctive because the whole account is past. iuvenes annos transfers the adjective: the years are called young, not the woman who would live them. protinus is “straight on”, and it can attach two ways. Taken with iuvenes ... annos it is “without a break”, so that what she failed to ask for is not youth once but youth continuing — which is exactly what Phoebus offers under the name aeterna iuventas at 140. Taken with peterem it is “at the same time”, and the failure is one of timing: she should have added this request while she was making the other. The literal follows the first, on the strength of 140. quoque here is the adverb “also”.

sentences.t:
Hos tamen ille mihi dabat aeternamque iuventam,
si venerem paterer:
sentences.l: These, however, he was giving me, and everlasting youth as well, if I would submit to the act of love:
sentences.i: Even so, he was ready to give me those years, and youth that never ended, if I would let him have me:
sentences.n: The offer is made twice over in these lines, and the tenses are the same both times: dabatur at 132 and dabat here, imperfect indicative for what was really being held out, with the unfulfilled condition in the subjunctive. The two conditional verbs only look like the same word: patuisset at 133 is from pateo, “lie open”, while paterer here is from patior, “submit to, put up with”, a deponent, passive in form and active in meaning. Hos picks up annos from the line before — the young years she had forgotten to ask for. ille is Phoebus, whom she leaves unnamed in this line and names in the next; she had last named him at 133. venus as a common noun is the sexual act itself, the goddess's name doing duty for the thing, and patior makes it something undergone rather than shared. The colon is Magnus's: the terms, and then her answer.

sentences.t:
contempto munere Phoebi
innuba permaneo;
sentences.l: with the gift of Phoebus held in contempt, I remain unwed;
sentences.i: I held Phoebus's gift in contempt, and unwed I remain;
sentences.n: contempto munere is an ablative absolute, “with the gift held in contempt”, where English wants a clause. The gift refused is the whole of the offer at 140: the young years she had forgotten to ask for and the everlasting youth, held out together on the one condition. It is not the birthdays she did ask for at 138 — those were granted outright and she keeps them, which is what the tally at 144 to 146 counts off. permaneo is a present among past tenses, and it is the point of the whole speech — the refusal was then, the state it left her in is now, which is what per- in permaneo carries. innuba is a poetic compound of in- and nubo, the verb used of a woman's marrying, so “unmarried” with the woman's side of the word built in.

sentences.t:
sed iam felicior aetas
terga dedit, tremuloque gradu venit aegra senectus,
quae patienda diu est (nam iam mihi saecula septem
acta vides):
sentences.l: but the happier time has already turned its back, and sick old age has come with trembling step, and it must be endured a long while (for you see that seven ages have already been lived out for me):
sentences.i: but my better years have already turned tail, and sick old age has come on with a shaking step, and there is a long stretch of it still to be borne — for you can see that seven ages of mine are already spent:
sentences.n: terga dare is the idiom for turning to run, so the good years are not merely gone but in flight. felicior is a comparative with nothing expressed to compare it to: happier than this. tremulo ... gradu is an ablative of manner, and aegra, “sick”, is put on old age itself rather than on the person. quae picks up senectus and carries the sentence on rather than defining her, which is why English wants “and it”; and patienda ... est is the passive periphrastic, gerundive with est: the thing that has to be undergone. saecula ... acta is an accusative and infinitive after vides with esse left out, and mihi is a dative of the person concerned — seven ages counted against her. A saeculum is a lifetime or generation, conventionally reckoned at a hundred years; on that reckoning the seven behind her and the three hundred still ahead in the next unit come to a thousand, though the poem never states the total. The parenthesis is Magnus's own punctuation, and Magnus prints vides, which turns it into an appeal to Aeneas's eyes; some editions print tamen there instead, which leaves it a flat statement addressed to nobody.

sentences.t:
superest, numeros ut pulveris aequem,
ter centum messes, ter centum musta videre.
sentences.l: it remains, so that I may match the numbers of the dust, to see three hundred harvests, three hundred vintages of new wine.
sentences.i: to make my count equal the dust's, I have still to see three hundred harvests and three hundred pressings of new wine.
sentences.n: superest with an infinitive is impersonal, “it is left over to”, and the infinitive videre that belongs to it is held back to the last word of the following line. ut is postponed behind numeros, which verse does freely, and aequem is a present subjunctive of purpose. ter centum, “three times a hundred”, is the poetic way of saying three hundred, and it is repeated because the year is being counted from both ends of its season: messes are the grain harvests of summer, musta the new wine of the autumn pressing. The two together name the same three hundred years twice, not six hundred.

sentences.t:
Tempus erit, cum de tanto me corpore parvam
longa dies faciet consumptaque membra senecta
ad minimum redigentur onus:
sentences.l: There will be a time when the long time will make me small out of so great a body, and my limbs, eaten away by old age, will be reduced to the least weight:
sentences.i: A time will come when the length of days will make me small out of a body so large, and my limbs, worn away by old age, will be brought down to the least of loads:
sentences.n: cum here takes the future indicative faciet, a plain temporal clause and not a subjunctive one. de tanto ... corpore is the ablative of the material a thing is made out of, and parvam is a predicate accusative agreeing with me: it will make me, small, out of that. dies is of either gender in Latin and is feminine here, as it regularly is when it means a stretch of time rather than a single day. consumpta is a perfect passive participle agreeing with membra, with senecta the ablative of the means. redigentur is future passive, “will be driven back, reduced”. onus is a weight or load, so the last of her is measured as something to be carried.

sentences.t:
nec amata videbor
nec placuisse deo;
sentences.l: I shall not seem to have been loved, nor to have pleased a god;
sentences.i: No one will think I was ever loved, or that I ever pleased a god;
sentences.n: videbor is the passive of video used personally, “I shall seem”, and it governs two perfect infinitives of different voices: amata, with esse left out, is passive, “to have been loved”, and placuisse is active, “to have pleased”. The pair covers both halves of it — that she was loved, and that she pleased. deo is left without a name, and the name follows immediately: Phoebus is the very next word.

sentences.t:
Phoebus quoque forsitan ipse
vel non cognoscet vel dilexisse negabit:
sentences.l: Phoebus himself too, perhaps, will either not recognise me, or will deny that he loved me:
sentences.i: Even Phoebus himself, perhaps, will either not know me, or will deny he ever loved me:
sentences.n: quoque is again the adverb “also”, not quo with -que, and ipse sharpens it: not strangers only, but the god in person. forsitan, “perhaps”, is normally construed with the subjunctive; here it stands with two future indicatives, cognoscet and negabit. vel ... vel sets out two possibilities as equally open, without preferring either. dilexisse is the perfect infinitive of diligo after negabit — Latin says “he will deny to have loved” where English needs a clause. diligo is the word for holding someone dear, not the hotter amo she used of herself in amata two lines earlier at 149, and the milder word is the one she puts into his mouth.

sentences.t:
usque adeo mutata ferar, nullique videnda,
voce tamen noscar;
sentences.l: So utterly changed shall I be borne along, and to be seen by no one, yet by my voice I shall be known;
sentences.i: So completely altered shall I be carried on, with no one to see me — but by my voice I shall still be known;
sentences.n: usque adeo, “to just that degree”, looks back: Magnus's colon at the end of 151 makes this the ground of what she has just said about Phoebus. ferar is the future passive of fero: the plainest sense is “I shall be borne along”, of a person carried on by time, though the passive of fero is also the Latin for “be reported, be spoken of”, and the line will bear either. mutata is a perfect passive participle agreeing with the subject: changed, and by nothing but time. nulli ... videnda is a gerundive with nulli as its dative of agent, “to be seen by no one”. tamen sets the voice against the body: everything that can be looked at goes, and the voice does not.

sentences.t: vocem mihi fata relinquent.”
sentences.l: my voice the fates will leave me.'
sentences.i: the fates will leave me my voice.'
sentences.n: The clause takes up voce from the clause before and repeats it as vocem, instrument turned into object, and puts it first in its own clause. mihi is the dative of the person a thing is left to. fata are the powers that fix what is allotted, and they are given the last verb of the speech; there is no adjective and no verb of being in the sentence, and the speech ends on the barest statement it could make.
